summary.text: Representability is unchanged when the two quadratic variables and their coefficients are swapped. Since the proposed list contains \((1,2,1,1)\) but omits its symmetric counterpart \((2,1,1,1)\), it cannot characterize representability by an equivalence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P(a,b,c,d)
\]
denote the assertion that \(a,b,c,d\) are positive integers and that every nonnegative integer \(n\) has a representation
\[
n=ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4
\]
with \(x,y,z,w\) nonnegative integers. Let \(S\) be the set of the 49 quadruples displayed in the conjecture. The conjecture asserts that, for every quadruple of nonnegative integers \((a,b,c,d)\),
\[
P(a,b,c,d)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (a,b,c,d)\in S.
\]
(The positivity requirement is already part of \(P\), so this formulation is equivalent to the stated formulation for positive coefficients.)

The key observation is that the two quadratic variables can be exchanged. More precisely, for all coefficients \(a,b,c,d\),
\[
P(a,b,c,d)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P(b,a,c,d).
\]
Indeed, suppose first that \(P(a,b,c,d)\) holds. The coefficients \(b,a,c,d\) are still positive. Given an arbitrary nonnegative integer \(n\), choose nonnegative integers \(x,y,z,w\) such that
\[
n=ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4.
\]
Set
\[
X=y,\qquad Y=x,\qquad Z=z,\qquad W=w.
\]
Then all four new variables are nonnegative and
\[
\begin{aligned}
bX^2+aY^2+cZ^3+dW^4
&=by^2+ax^2+cz^3+dw^4\\
&=ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4\\
&=n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(P(b,a,c,d)\) holds. Applying the same exchange once more proves the converse. Hence full representability is symmetric in the first two coefficients.

Now consider the two coefficient quadruples
\[
q=(1,2,1,1),\qquad q'=(2,1,1,1).
\]
The quadruple \(q\) occurs in the conjecture's displayed list—in fact, it is the first listed quadruple—so
\[
(1,2,1,1)\in S.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
(2,1,1,1)\notin S.
\]
This is a direct finite inspection of the displayed list. For completeness, the entries in that list whose first coordinate is \(2\) are
\[
(2,3,1,1),\ (2,4,1,1),\ (2,4,1,2),\ (2,3,1,4),\ (2,3,1,5),\ (2,4,1,5),\ (2,4,1,11).
\]
None has second coordinate \(1\), and therefore none is \((2,1,1,1)\).

Assume, for contradiction, that the conjectured equivalence holds for every quadruple. Applying its right-to-left direction to the listed quadruple \((1,2,1,1)\) gives
\[
P(1,2,1,1).
\]
Explicitly, under the conjecture this says that every nonnegative integer is representable in the form
\[
x^2+2y^2+z^3+w^4.
\]
By the symmetry just proved, exchanging the two quadratic variables gives
\[
P(2,1,1,1).
\]
Thus every nonnegative integer is also representable in the form
\[
2x^2+y^2+z^3+w^4.
\]
Applying the conjectured equivalence to \((2,1,1,1)\), now in its left-to-right direction, forces
\[
(2,1,1,1)\in S.
\]
But the finite inspection above showed that \((2,1,1,1)\notin S\). This contradiction proves that the proposed equivalence cannot hold for all positive coefficient quadruples.

Equivalently, one may express the same obstruction as a two-case argument independent of knowing which particular representability assertion fails. Either \(P(1,2,1,1)\) is false, in which case the conjecture is already false because \((1,2,1,1)\) is listed; or \(P(1,2,1,1)\) is true, in which case symmetry makes \(P(2,1,1,1)\) true even though \((2,1,1,1)\) is omitted. In either case the claimed classification by the 49 displayed quadruples is false.
